title: A training curve is a diary: read the slope, the spikes and the gap, not just the last value
summary: Four Playground figures draw loss or accuracy against epoch: an eleven-optimizer race on a small Van der Pol benchmark, a train-versus-validation tour, a linear readout against a decoder head, and an initialization failure. The same habits apply to each: log axis, same budget, look for plateaus and spikes.

media.alt: Line chart titled optimizer race on the Van der Pol synthetic benchmark, eleven coloured curves of training loss on a log axis from about ten down to about one over eighty epochs. Slow curves sit near ten; fast ones drop in the first twenty epochs and show sharp spikes around epochs forty to fifty-five. The legend lists start and final loss for each optimizer.

read_the_figure.question: Which training run reaches a low loss reliably, and what do its plateaus and spikes say about how it got there?
read_the_figure.axes: Horizontal: epoch (0 to 80 in the race, 0 to 60 in the tour). Vertical: train loss on a log scale (about 0.6 to 12). The legend of the race prints each optimizer's first and last loss, for example 'Nadam (9.82 -> 0.696)'.
look_at: Slopes first: a steep early drop (RMSprop, Rprop, Nadam) means fast initial progress; a near-flat curve (Adadelta, L-BFGS, SGD here) means almost no learning in this budget.

Spikes: several curves jump up by a factor of two to three around epochs 40 to 45 and again near 54. Adam and AdamW (identical here, so one curve hides the other) show this most clearly. The tour figure shows the same spikes in both train and validation loss.

The gap between train and validation (tour figure): the two curves track each other until the spikes, so there is no overfitting gap here; the spikes are optimization events, not generalization effects.
The decoder-head figure compares a linear readout and an MLP decoder: the decoder starts lower and is calmer; the linear head spikes at the same epochs.

The initialization figure: validation accuracy against epoch for zero and non-zero initialization, with the chance line at 0.5. One curve rises to 1.0 in about eight epochs; the other stays at or below chance for the whole run.
read_the_figure.proves: Final loss alone hides the story. The shape tells which run is fast, which is fragile, and whether a failure is slow learning (a flat line), instability (spikes), or a structural problem (zero initialization pinned at chance).
if_wrong: Same seed and budget but different data: the race is not a comparison.
A single seed: spikes and rank order can change with the seed, so rankings from one run are suggestive only.
A flat curve at chance (0.5 for two classes): symmetry was never broken or the learning rate is zero.
A spike followed by recovery to the old level: a transient instability; one that does not recover is divergence.
must_check: That the vertical axis is log when the loss spans a decade or more.
That each curve has the same epoch budget, seed and data (the title states it).
That several seeds are shown before ranking optimizers.
That the metric (train loss, validation loss, accuracy) is on the axis label.

terms.meaning: One pass over the training data.
The rule that turns a gradient into a parameter update: SGD, Adam, RMSprop and so on.
An optimizer that scales steps by running averages of the gradient and its square.
The overall step size of the update.
Giving different hidden units different starting weights so they can learn different features.
Validation loss above training loss; it grows when the model memorises.
The accuracy of random guessing, 0.5 for two balanced classes.

remember: Use a log axis for loss; equal vertical distances then mean equal factors.
Compare optimizers at equal seed, epochs and learning-rate effort.
A spike in both train and validation loss is an optimizer event; a growing gap between them is overfitting.
If all hidden units start identical they receive identical gradients and stay identical.
A single run is an anecdote; report several seeds.

steps.title: Reading a log axis as a factor
steps.note: Vertical distance on the plot is the number of decades gained. Nadam goes from 9.82 to 0.696, a factor of 14 (1.15 decades).

steps.title: Why Adam can jump after a quiet stretch
steps.note: When gradients have been small for a while the running estimate of their square is tiny, so a sudden large gradient makes a large step. A common explanation of loss spikes; the figure alone cannot prove it.

steps.title: Zero initialization cannot break symmetry
steps.tex: \hat y=\sum_j v_j\,\sigma(w_j\!\cdot x)\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_j}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\hat y}\,v_j\,\sigma'(w_j\!\cdot x)\,x
steps.note: If every v_j and w_j start equal (or v_j = 0), all hidden units get the same (or zero) gradient and remain identical for ever: the network behaves like one unit. Validation accuracy stays near chance.

steps.title: Train and validation share an optimizer event
steps.note: If both curves jump at the same epoch, the parameters moved; the gap term did not. That separates optimizer instability from overfitting.

worked.title: How many decades did the best optimizer gain?
worked.problem: The race legend shows Nadam 9.82 -> 0.696 and SGD 9.99 -> 2.323. Compare the gains.
worked.answer: Nadam gains 1.15 decades (factor 14), SGD 0.63 decades (factor 4.3), for the same 80 epochs and seed.

analyze.q: Which two curves in the race are identical in the plot and what does that suggest about their settings?
analyze.hint: Adam and AdamW without weight decay.

analyze.q: Spikes occur at about the same epochs for several optimizers. What does that suggest: optimizer or data? How would you test it?
analyze.hint: Change the seed or the batch order.

analyze.q: Explain why a model with zero initialization stays at or below chance although it trains for 80 epochs.

evaluate.q: Rank the eleven optimizers from this figure alone. Which claim would you refuse to make?
evaluate.hint: One seed, one benchmark, one budget.

evaluate.q: Is the final epoch the right place to read the loss? Argue using the spikes.

create: Design a version of the race that reports median and spread over ten seeds and shows the best-so-far curve as a thin line.
Make a three-panel figure that separates slow learning, instability and a structural failure, each with a one-line verdict in the title.

checks.q: Why plot loss on a log axis?
checks.hint: What do equal vertical steps mean?
checks.answer: Equal vertical distances correspond to equal factors, so a decade of improvement looks the same anywhere on the curve.

checks.q: Loss falls from 9.8 to 0.7. How many decades?
Train and validation both spike at epoch 43. Overfitting?
checks.answer: No. Overfitting is a growing gap between the curves; here both move together, so the parameters took a bad step.

checks.q: One optimizer wins by 10 percent in a single run. Do you switch?
checks.answer: Not on that evidence: the spikes show run-to-run variation of a factor of two or three, larger than 10 percent.

checks.q: Propose a fix when Adam spikes late in training.
checks.answer: Lower the learning rate on a schedule, clip gradients, or raise epsilon; then re-run with several seeds to check the spikes are gone.
